---
title: "Serve a Lab to an agent"
description: "Let any MCP agent use a Lab's tools, with every action checked, approved and recorded by the same rules as your evaluations."
---

Evaluations test what an agent does in a Lab. Serving a Lab lets an agent use it
outside an evaluation, with the same safeguards. Every tool call goes through the
**gateway**: it is checked against your rules, held for approval if needed, and
recorded, before it reaches the Lab. The same rule file decides the same way in an
evaluation and when served.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Prototype
Serving has been tested with simulated and mock Labs only. It has not been used with
real instruments, and it is not a substitute for facility safety controls.
:::

## Serve a Lab

Install the optional extra, then serve a registered Lab over MCP's stdio transport:

```bash
uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python '.[serve]'
inspect-labs serve --lab liquid-handler \
  --rules rules.json --approvals approvals.json \
  --stop-file .research/STOP --lab-log .research/session.json
```

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| `--lab` | A registered Lab (see `inspect-labs list`) |
| `--rules` | Action rules as JSON. Without it, the default rules allow reads and reversible actions and hold irreversible and external actions for approval. |
| `--approvals` | Actions a person approved in advance, as a JSON list of `{"tool": ..., "arguments": {...}}`. A held action runs only if it matches one exactly. |
| `--stop-file` | Stop the session when this file appears. Every later action is refused, and the file's text is recorded as the reason. |
| `--lab-log` | Where to write the session's lab log when the agent disconnects. It is never overwritten. |
| `--leases` | Time-limited permissions given in advance, as a JSON list of `{name, tool, match, expires_at, uses, granted_by}`. |
| `--control-socket` | A private local socket operators use to watch, approve and stop the session while it runs. Held actions then wait for an operator. |
| `--approval-timeout` | Seconds a held action waits for an operator before it is refused (default 300). |
| `--refusal-limit` | Stop the session after this many refused actions. |
| `--stop-on` | Stop the session when this live monitor flags. Repeat for several. |
| `--journal` | Where to write each step as it happens. Defaults to the lab log path with `.journal.jsonl`. |
| `--witness-file` | Also append each journal digest here. Keep it where the lab can't rewrite it. |

Point any MCP agent at the command. For example, in an MCP client configuration:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "lab": {
      "command": "inspect-labs",
      "args": ["serve", "--lab", "liquid-handler", "--lab-log", "session.json"]
    }
  }
}
```

The agent sees the Lab's tools. A refused action comes back as an error with the
reason, and never reaches the Lab. The agent cannot stop or reconfigure the gateway.

## Operators in the loop

With `--control-socket`, a held action waits for a person instead of being refused
at once. Operators answer from another terminal:

```bash
inspect-labs operator .research/ops/lab.sock pending
inspect-labs operator .research/ops/lab.sock approve 3f9c1a2b7d4e --by alice
inspect-labs operator .research/ops/lab.sock stop --by alice --reason "Unexpected plan"
```

- Every answer records who gave it, and the lab log shows it as `approved_by`.
- An action nobody answers in time is refused. Nobody answering is not approval.
- A stop refuses everything still waiting, and wins over an approval that arrives
  after it.
- The socket's directory must be private (mode 700), so only the operator's own
  account can use it. The agent's tools never include it, so an agent can't approve
  its own actions or lift a stop.

## Tripwires

Monitors also run after every action while the session runs. `--refusal-limit 3`
stops the session after three refused actions, since an agent repeatedly hitting the
rules may be probing them. `--stop-on irreversible-without-approval` stops it the
first time that monitor flags.

## The journal

The lab log is written when the session ends. The journal is written as the session
happens: each decision before the action reaches the Lab, then any approval, the
result, stops and flags. Each line is flushed to disk before the gateway continues,
so a crash loses at most the line being written.

```bash
inspect-labs journal .research/session.journal.jsonl --witness /mnt/witness/lab.txt
```

Each entry is hash-chained to the one before it, so changing, removing or reordering
an entry is detected. Someone with write access could still rebuild the whole file.
A witness file closes that gap if it lives somewhere they can't rewrite, such as
another machine or an append-only store: a rebuilt journal no longer matches it.
Each journal starts with a random id, and witness lines name it, so one witness file
can serve many sessions. A journal the witness has no record of is reported too.

## After the session

The session's lab log records every action, the decision, any approval and whether
it ran, then what the Lab reported. It is hash-chained like an evaluation's lab log,
and includes monitor flags such as refused actions.

```bash
inspect-labs replay-rules .research/session.json --rules new-rules.json
```

Replaying rules works the same on a session's lab log as on an evaluation's: it shows
what the new rules would have decided, without running anything.

## From Python

```python
from inspect_labs import DEFAULT_RULES
from inspect_labs.gateway import ApprovedAction, approved_actions
from inspect_labs.serve import LabSession, serve_over_stdio

session = LabSession(
    my_lab,
    DEFAULT_RULES,
    approver=approved_actions([ApprovedAction(tool="drop_tip", arguments={})]),
)
# session.stop("reason") refuses every later action.
```
